messages.content:
The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighLatency on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: p95 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T02:16:07Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T02:16:29Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came 7 minutes 7 seconds {detection_gap} after its series passed its line, within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
Broken from 2026-11-11T02:08:00Z {began} (the onset) to 2026-11-11T02:16:57Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 8 minutes 57 seconds {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 2 minutes 33 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T02:19:01Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.1% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 1.1% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 2.0% {errors_at_worst} - no higher than the worst minutes of stretches as long before it began.
Rise above baseline: none beyond its normal variation - stretches as long before it began averaged as high on their own.
The series behind the alert, `max(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.95"}) * 1000` - its alert said "p95 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 214.18333333333334 ms {series_before} before it began, 1314.625 ms {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 1811 ms {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
No rise in failed requests was measured, so the harm to report is what this series did: say what it meant for the people using the service, not that little or nothing failed.
Customer loss: none - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all.

What Argus did, in order:
  - [T1] 2026-11-11T02:16:28Z {T1.1} Argus: Received HighLatency on io-shop
  - [T2] 2026-11-11T02:16:36Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
  - [T3] 2026-11-11T02:16:36Z {T3.1} Argus: Called in the Investigator Agent
  - [T4] 2026-11-11T02:16:43Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 02:16:07 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-11-11T02:16:47Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 360 {T5.2} minutes of metrics
  - [T6] 2026-11-11T02:16:49Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 02:08 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-11-11T02:16:49Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 {T7.2} replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
  - [T8] 2026-11-11T02:16:50Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 {T8.2} day 1 {T8.3} minute before Nov 11 02:09 {T8.4}
  - [T9] 2026-11-11T02:16:51Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 0 {T9.2} production changes
  - [T10] 2026-11-11T02:16:51Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 {T10.2} replicas run one revision, which the history does not name
  - [T11] 2026-11-11T02:16:52Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 1 {T11.2} candidate cause, best first: C1
  - [T12] 2026-11-11T02:16:52Z {T12.1} Investigator Agent: Did not read logs
  - [T13] 2026-11-11T02:16:52Z {T13.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 0 {T13.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T13.3} hour before 02:16:52 {T13.4}
  - [T14] 2026-11-11T02:16:56Z {T14.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate
  - [T15] 2026-11-11T02:16:56Z {T15.1} Argus: Called in the Mitigation Agent
  - [T16] 2026-11-11T02:16:57Z {T16.1} Mitigation Agent: Scaled out the deployment of io-shop for C1
  - [T17] 2026-11-11T02:17:04Z {T17.1} Mitigation Agent: Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 02:17 {T17.2} - up to 182s {T17.3}
  - [T18] 2026-11-11T02:19:01Z {T18.1} Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 02:16 {T18.2}
  - [T19] 2026-11-11T02:19:01Z {T19.1} Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
  - [T20] 2026-11-11T02:19:01Z {T20.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATED - scaled [io-shop] out from [3 {T20.2}] replicas and the rule that fired stopped firing
  - [T21] 2026-11-11T02:20:34Z {T21.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/529

Changes to production it read:
  - Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - Not read.

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] Request volume ramped from 1200/min {C1.1} starting 2026-11-11T02:03:00Z {C1.2} to 5400/min {C1.3}, about 4.5 {C1.4} times baseline. CPU use rose with it and hit the fixed 3.0-core limit at 2026-11-11T02:11:00Z {C1.5}. Requests then queued for CPU, and p95 rose from about 210 {C1.6} ms to over 1800 {C1.7} ms. Nothing was deployed or changed, and the rollout had converged. [demand-saturation, confidence 0.85 {C1.8}, confirmed]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Scaled out the deployment of io-shop for [C1] (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place

What the metrics show of the confirmed cause [C1], measured by Argus:
  - [R1] Requests: 1200/min {R1.1} before it began, 4841/min {R1.2} on average while it was broken, 5400/min {R1.3} at its highest.
  - [R2] CPU in use, as a share of the service's CPU limit: 25.0% {R2.1} before it began, 94.7% {R2.2} on average while it was broken, 100.0% {R2.3} at its highest.
  - The record confirmed [C1]: the load outgrew the CPU the service had, and adding capacity ended it. What changed before it began was the load, not the service, so the load against that CPU is the root cause; a reading that would make requests cheaper is at most a contributing factor.

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The investigation found CPU rising in step with request volume until it hit the fixed 3.0-core limit, and nothing deployed or changed. That makes CPU cost per request the thing this code controls. Both functions in the account page's figure path do quadratic work for each request:
      
      - `average_spend_per_item` in `src/io_shop/spend_summary.py` is the default figure, rendered for every request outside the rollouts. For each purchase it re-sums the whole prefix `account.purchases[:index + 1]`, then throws away every sum except the last. That is n(n+1)/2 price reads plus n slice copies to get one total, which a single `sum` over the purchases gives. The fix sums once. The result is unchanged: it is still derived from the purchases, not from the carried `total_cents`. An empty history still raises `ZeroDivisionError` (0 {F1.1} // 0 {F1.2}), which the existing boundary test relies on.
      - `typical_spend_per_item` in `src/io_shop/typical_spend.py` (behind `typical-purchase-feature`) runs `min` and `remove` over the remaining list about n/2 times, which is also O(n²). The fix sorts once and indexes the lower middle, `(n - 1 {F1.3}) // 2`. That picks the same element the old loop did, including repeated prices and the lower middle of an even-length history. An empty history still raises `ValueError`, as the old `min([])` did.
      
      The more history a shopper has, the faster per-request cost grew, so the pods hit the CPU limit at a much lower request rate than the work needs. This change doesn't remove the fixed limit or the autoscaling settings in `deploy/values-production.yaml`. It cuts how much CPU each page costs, so the same cores serve more requests before they queue. Nothing has run these changes or the tests; the claims below come from reading the code.
      
      Tests:
      - `tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py` adds a case that counts reads of `price_cents` over a 1000-purchase history and asserts at most 2n. The old prefix re-summing does about 500,000 {F1.4} reads.
      - `tests/io_shop/test_typical_spend.py` adds a case that counts `<` comparisons between prices over a shuffled 1000-purchase history and asserts fewer than 50,000 {F1.5}. A single sort needs about n log n (roughly 10,000 {F1.6}); the old repeated `min` needs several hundred thousand. Both new tests also check that the answer is still right, and the existing correctness tests are kept unchanged.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Scaled out the deployment of io-shop
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
  - AI-3 (mitigate, open): Turn automatic sync of io-shop back on once its repository says what should run - until then nothing merged reaches it, and turned on sooner it puts back what the repository says, undoing what Argus changed by hand
PR #529 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: Requests to io-shop climbed from {R1.1} to as high as {R1.3}, and CPU use climbed with them until it reached the service's CPU limit ({R2.3} at its highest). From then on the replicas had more work than CPU to do it, so requests waited for CPU and responses slowed.
cause_in_plain_words: The shop got far more requests than usual, more than its servers had the computing power to handle at once, so requests had to wait their turn.
still_at_risk: If requests rise beyond what the scaled-out replicas' CPU can handle, io-shop could run out of CPU again and slow down the same way.
symptom: Shop pages slowed sharply for shoppers
causal_chain 1: Responses from io-shop slowed sharply. The time within which nearly all requests are answered rose far above its usual level, so shoppers waited much longer for pages. (cites AL1)
causal_chain 2: Requests were waiting for CPU: the service was using all of the CPU its limit allowed. (cites R2, under "What the metrics show of the confirmed cause [C1], measured by Argus")
causal_chain 3: CPU use reached that limit because requests rose to several times their level before the onset and CPU use rose in step with them. That was more load than the replicas' CPU could handle. (cites R1, under "What the metrics show of the confirmed cause [C1], measured by Argus"; R2, under "What the metrics show of the confirmed cause [C1], measured by Argus")
contributing_factors 1: No replicas were seen being added automatically as CPU use reached its limit. The service stayed at {T20.2} replicas until Argus scaled it out.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: Capacity would have grown as the load did. That would have kept requests from queuing for CPU, or cut the queuing short.
contributing_factors 2: Each request likely cost more CPU than it needed to. Code-Fix read the files behind the account page's spending figures: the default figure, and the one behind typical-purchase-feature, both do work that grows with the square of a shopper's purchase history. Nothing has run this reading.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: Cheaper requests would have let the same CPU handle more of them before they queued, so the slowdown would have been later and milder, or would not have happened.
contributing_factors 3: No alert was seen when CPU use neared its limit. The slowdown was found only by the latency alert, which waits {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires.
contributing_factors 3 had_it_been_otherwise: An alert on CPU nearing its limit could have fired before latency rose this far, so capacity could have been added sooner.
action_items 1: Configure io-shop to add replicas automatically as CPU use nears its limit, with enough room for at least the peak request rate seen in this incident ({R1.3}).
action_items 2: Add an alert on io-shop's CPU use as a share of its CPU limit, so the service is flagged when it nears saturation and before latency climbs.
action_items 3: Make the HighLatency alert on io-shop page the on-call engineer.
action_items 4: Find where the rise in requests to io-shop came from, and whether it can happen again at this size or larger.
went_wrong 1: Nobody was paged: the alert did not open an on-call incident, so no person was engaged.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.

tools.name: judge_claims
